recipe.history:
Long before European settlers arrived on the American continent, corn and acorns were two of the most vital staples sustaining Indigenous peoples across North America. Corn — or maize — was first domesticated by the Olmec and Maya civilizations in southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago, and through centuries of careful cultivation it spread north to become the backbone of countless Native American agricultural traditions, from the Three Sisters planting system of the Haudenosaunee to the dried hominy preparations of the Cherokee. Acorns, meanwhile, were a parallel cornerstone: ground into flour and leached of their bitter tannins, they formed the basis of breads, porridges, and stews from the Miwok of California to the Lenape of the Eastern Woodlands. The name "A-CORN-PLISHED" revels in this dual heritage — a pun that collapses acorn and corn into a single triumphant word, a culinary salute to two ingredients that fed an entire continent long before the hamburger was even a glimmer in anyone's eye.

As American foodways evolved through the 18th and 19th centuries, corn never strayed far from the center of the national table — cornbread, grits, succotash, and eventually the sweet corn relishes and salsas that began appearing at summer cookouts and roadside stands. The backyard burger, itself a 20th-century American institution, proved to be a willing canvas for corn's bright sweetness. Charred corn salsas and roasted corn relishes became popular burger toppings in the Southwestern United States, lending smoky, caramelized complexity to beef patties. Acorn squash, a more distant relative of the acorn's earthy nuttiness, followed its own arc into American comfort cooking — roasted, pureed, or sliced thin, its sweetness bridges the gap between autumn harvests and the satisfying heft of a well-built burger. Together, these two ingredients carry centuries of agricultural memory onto a brioche bun.

The first time I made this burger, it was late October — that precise window when the air smells like woodsmoke and the farmers' markets are stacked high with hard squash and the last of the sweet corn. I stood at the grill in a flannel shirt with a cold can of something nearby, and when I lifted the lid and the steam rolled out carrying that smell of charred beef and caramelized corn, it hit me like a photograph I hadn't looked at in years. It reminded me of my grandmother's kitchen, where she kept a cast-iron skillet permanently seasoned with decades of use, and how she'd throw corn in dry and let it blacken at the edges before folding it into everything. This burger is that feeling made edible — nostalgia with a crust on it, humble ingredients doing something quietly extraordinary.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a burger like this, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. At medium rare, the beef is still blushing pink at the center, the fat has begun to render but not fully escape, and every bite carries the full, iron-rich depth that a quality beef blend was meant to deliver. Cook it further and you are not cooking — you are punishing. The sweetness of the corn salsa and the earthiness of the acorn squash spread are calibrated against that specific temperature; they are condiments designed for a living patty, not a dry one. Medium rare is not a preference here. It is the philosophy of respecting your ingredients all the way to the final degree.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
FOR THE BEEF PATTY BLEND (makes 4 patties):
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef chuck (80/20 fat ratio)
2 ears of fresh sweet corn, husked
1 medium acorn squash (about 900g), halved and seeded
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
Neutral oil or clarified butter, for the griddle or grill grates
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the 2 eggs and warm milk. Mix on low for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms.

2. Increase mixer speed to medium and knead for 5 minutes. With the mixer running, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to incorporate before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes. The dough should be smooth, glossy, and slightly tacky.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours). Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the dough easier to shape.

4. The next day, remove dough from the refrigerator and let it sit at room temperature for 1 hour. Divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 155g each). Shape each into a tight round ball by pulling the dough surface down and pinching it underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart.
5. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 2–3 hours until visibly puffed and pillowy. Preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C.

6. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water. Gently brush the tops of the buns with egg wash. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 18–22 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack for at least 30 minutes before slicing.

7. MAKE THE ACORN SQUASH SPREAD: Preheat oven to 400°F / 205°C. Place acorn squash halves cut-side up on a baking sheet. Place 1 tbsp butter and half the maple syrup in the cavity of each half. Roast for 45–55 minutes until the flesh is completely tender and caramelized at the edges.

8. Scoop the flesh into a food processor or blender. Add the cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, salt, apple cider vinegar, and any caramelized juices from the pan. Blend until completely smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning. Transfer to a bowl and refrigerate until needed. This spread can be made up to 3 days ahead.

9. MAKE THE CHARRED CORN SALSA: Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill to very high heat. Rub the corn ears lightly with neutral oil. Char the corn directly on the grill or in the dry cast-iron skillet, turning every 2–3 minutes, until deeply blackened in spots on all sides — about 12 minutes total. Let cool.

10. Cut the kernels from the cobs by standing each ear upright on a cutting board and slicing downward with a sharp knife. Combine corn kernels, red onion, jalapeño, garlic, lime juice, cilantro, cumin, smoked paprika, and salt in a bowl. Toss well. Taste and adjust lime juice and salt. Let sit at room temperature for at least 20 minutes for the flavors to meld.

11. MAKE THE HERB AIOLI: In a medium bowl, whisk together the egg yolks, Dijon mustard, and garlic paste until pale and slightly thickened. Whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in an extremely thin, steady stream — drop by drop at first — until the emulsion forms and thickens. Once roughly half the oil is incorporated, you can add the remaining oil in a slow, thin stream.
12. Stir in the lemon juice, chives, parsley, salt, and white pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning. If the aioli is too thick, thin it with 1–2 tsp cold water. Refrigerate until ready to use.

13. PREPARE THE BEEF PATTIES: Combine the ground chuck and ground short rib in a large bowl. Mix gently with your hands — just enough to combine. Do not overwork the meat. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 200g each). Form each into a patty roughly 4.5 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper right before cooking. Do not season in advance.

14. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking, or heat a grill to high. Lightly oil the cooking surface. Place patties on the cooking surface and do not press or move them for 3 minutes. Flip once. Cook for 2–3 more minutes on the second side. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — you are targeting 130–135°F / 54–57°C at the center. Remove from heat and tent loosely with foil. Rest for 3–4 minutes. The carryover cooking will bring the internal temp up slightly; do not exceed 135°F.

15. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice the brioche buns in half. Butter the cut sides lightly and place face-down on the same griddle or skillet over medium heat. Toast for 1–2 minutes until golden and crisp. Remove immediately.

16. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous layer of acorn squash spread on the bottom bun. Place a leaf of green leaf lettuce over the spread. Layer 2 slices of tomato on the lettuce. Place the rested patty on the tomatoes. Spoon a heaping tablespoon of charred corn salsa directly onto the patty. Add a dollop of herb aioli on the top bun. Press the top bun gently onto the burger. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt over the exposed salsa.
17. Serve immediately. This burger waits for no one.
